body.x: Most couples arrive at their nikah knowing the celebration better than the contract. Yet the nikah is a contract — a solemn one — and in Shia Islam its validity rests on a small number of clear essentials. Get those right and the ceremony around them can be as simple or as festive as a family wishes. This guide covers permanent nikah, the lifelong marriage that Shia Rishta exists to serve. Where the marjas differ on a detail, that is said openly; for anything touching your own marriage, your own marja's ruling is the one that governs.
Consent comes first — and it must be real

No nikah is valid without the free consent of both the woman and the man. A contract recited over a reluctant bride or a pressured groom is not a marriage in the eyes of the Sharia, whatever the paperwork says. Consent is expressed through the contract itself: each side either recites the formula personally or appoints a representative (wakil) to recite it on their behalf, and that appointment is itself an act of consent. Families can advise, persuade and even plead — but the yes must belong to the two people marrying. One further rule surprises many families: for a woman who has never been married, most marjas also require the permission of her father or paternal grandfather. The precise scope of this rule, and its exceptions, differ between marjas, so it is a question to settle with yours well before the day, not during it.
The aqd: the words that make the marriage

The marriage is created by the sigha — the formula of offer and acceptance, ijab and qabul. In Twelver Shia fiqh the formula is recited in Arabic, and it matters that it is recited correctly: this is why most families ask a scholar or an experienced reciter to lead it, checking the wording in advance rather than improvising on the day. In the standard form, the bride's side offers her in marriage to the groom for the agreed mahr, and the groom's side accepts — immediately, in the same sitting, in words that clearly refer to this marriage and this mahr. There is no gap in which the couple are half-married: before the acceptance they are non-mahram to each other, and after it they are husband and wife. Because the wording carries this much weight, couples should know in advance who is reciting, in what order, and on whose behalf.

The bride and groom may recite the formula themselves, and some couples choose to. More commonly, each appoints a wakil — often a scholar acting for one or both sides, with the explicit permission of the person they represent. A wakil is not a formality: he can only say what he has been authorised to say, including the exact mahr agreed. Whoever recites, two things must be true before the first word is spoken: the mahr has been fixed, and both sides know precisely what is about to be agreed. If a scholar is officiating, give him the names, the mahr and any agreed conditions in writing beforehand. Mistakes in names or figures, recited in a noisy hall, are the commonest avoidable problem at real nikahs.
Witnesses: required for the record, not for validity

Here Shia fiqh differs from the Sunni schools, and families from mixed backgrounds are often surprised. In Twelver Shia law, witnesses are not a condition for the validity of the nikah contract itself — the marriage is valid on the correctly recited aqd with consent and the specified mahr. (Witnesses are required for a divorce, which is a separate matter.) That said, having trustworthy witnesses present is wise and customary: they anchor the marriage in the community's memory, and civil registration in many countries asks for them. Publicity has its own value in Islam — a marriage announced is a marriage protected — so treat witnesses as an important part of the occasion even though the contract does not stand or fall on them.
Mahr and conditions: what goes inside the contract

The mahr — the bridal gift that is the wife's exclusive right — must be specified in the contract, whether it is paid promptly, deferred, or split between the two. Alongside the mahr, a couple may write lawful conditions (shurut) into the contract: matters such as where they will live, the wife continuing her education or work, or other agreed arrangements. A condition that is written in, lawful and accepted becomes binding as part of the contract itself, which is why conditions should be discussed calmly during the rishta stage rather than raised for the first time at the ceremony. Standard printed forms leave limited room for conditions, so anything important should be agreed in advance and, where needed, recorded properly with the officiant's help.
Permanent nikah and temporary marriage are not the same contract

Readers will encounter references to mut'ah and should understand the distinction factually. Twelver Shia fiqh recognises, alongside permanent marriage, a temporary marriage contract in which a fixed duration and a mahr are agreed at the outset and the marriage ends when the term expires. Sunni schools do not recognise this contract. Within Shia scholarship it is a real but tightly ruled arrangement, with its own conditions — including the same requirements of consent and, where applicable, a guardian's permission — and it is surrounded by strong social sensitivities in most communities. It is not a casual or informal relationship, and it is not what this guide, or Shia Rishta, is about: everything here concerns permanent nikah, entered with lifelong intent. Anyone with questions about either contract should put them to a qualified scholar rather than rely on internet summaries, this one included.

Free consent of both the woman and the man
Guardian's permission where your marja requires it
A fixed mahr, stated in the contract
The aqd recited correctly in Arabic, by the couple or their authorised representatives
Offer and acceptance in the same sitting, referring to this marriage
Any agreed conditions settled beforehand and written in
Civil registration completed according to your country's law

None of this is bureaucracy for its own sake. The rules exist so that two people begin married life with a clear, witnessed, unpressured yes — and everything after the aqd is built on that foundation.

excerpt: The rules that actually make a Shia nikah valid — consent, the aqd formula, who may recite it, witnesses, mahr and contract conditions — explained plainly, with the differences between marjas flagged honestly.
title: Shia nikah rules: the essentials
